title: Peat and Smoke in Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: Where the smoky taste in some whiskies comes from, how peat levels are measured and why the smoke fades as the whisky ages.
teaser: That smoky, medicinal whisky everyone either loves or hates? The smoke went in before the barley was even brewed.
standfirst: Smoky whisky divides a room faster than almost any other drink. This guide explains what peat is, how its smoke ends up in the glass and why peat levels on a malt spec do not translate neatly into the bottle.
sections:
Peat is partly decayed plant matter that builds up very slowly in waterlogged bogs. It forms over thousands of years from mosses, heather, grasses and roots. Cut into blocks and dried, it burns with a thick, aromatic smoke. In parts of Scotland and Ireland where there were few trees, peat was the household fuel for centuries.

Distillers in those places dried their malted barley over peat fires because that was the fuel they had. The smoke flavoured the grain. What began as a matter of necessity became a style.
How the smoke gets into the grain

Whisky starts as malted barley, grain that has been soaked, allowed to sprout and then dried in a kiln. For peated whisky, peat is burned early in the kiln cycle while the grain is still damp. Wet grain picks up smoke far better than dry grain, so the timing matters.

The flavour comes from compounds called phenols in the smoke. They stick to the husk and the grain. After that the kiln usually switches to a cleaner heat source to finish drying. Our guide to how whisky is made follows the malt from there into the still.

Maltsters measure peating level as phenol content in parts per million, written as ppm. As a rough guide, lightly peated malt sits in single figures, medium peated in the teens to twenties and heavily peated malt from around 30 to 50 ppm. Some distilleries go much higher.

Here is the catch for anyone reading specs. The ppm figure describes the malt, not the whisky. A large share of the phenols is lost during mashing, fermentation and especially distillation. Where the distiller makes the cut between the heart of the run and the tails changes how much smoke survives, because many of the heavier phenols come over late. Two distilleries using identical malt can make spirits with very different smokiness.
Why the smoke fades with age

Peat character is strongest in young spirit. As the whisky sits in oak, the wood adds sweetness, vanilla and spice, while some of the sharper smoky compounds soften. A young peated whisky can taste like a bonfire. The same spirit after many more years often tastes more like smoked fruit or old leather.

This is useful context for anyone who works with portfolio or pricing data. A younger peated whisky is not simply a cheaper version of an older one. It is a deliberately different flavour.
Smoke without peat, and peat in India

Not every smoky note comes from peat. Casks that once held heavily peated whisky pass some of that character on. Charred oak casks give toasty, roasted notes that people sometimes read as smoke. Blenders mix peated and unpeated whiskies to set a precise level for a brand, which is part of how blenders keep brands consistent.

Indian distilleries that make peated single malts commonly import peated malt, often from Scotland, since India has no tradition of cutting peat for malting. That ties a peated product to import lead times and currency in a way an unpeated one is not.

The Scottish island of Islay is the best-known home of heavily peated whisky, with a maritime character often described as iodine, seaweed or tar. Peat cut on the Scottish mainland, rich in heather, tends to give a sweeter, earthier smoke. The plants that formed the peat shape its smoke, so peat from different bogs gives different flavours even at the same ppm.

Smoky whisky is a minority style. Most Scotch blends and most Indian whisky carry little or no peat. Many drinkers never meet a heavily peated malt at all. That is why it is worth knowing before a client dinner or a product briefing: the same word, smoky, can describe a faint wisp or a mouthful of bonfire.

If your team wants to understand peat, a side by side comparison of an unpeated malt, a lightly peated one and a heavily peated one teaches more in twenty minutes than any slide. Keep it opt-in and within company policy, pour small measures, provide water and spit cups and make sure non-drinkers can join by smelling the glasses. Most of what peat does can be learned through the nose.
faqs: What gives some whiskies a smoky taste?
Usually peat smoke absorbed by the barley while it was dried in the kiln. Phenols from the smoke stick to the grain and some survive into the spirit.
What does ppm mean for peated whisky?
Parts per million of phenols, measured in the malt. It describes the malt, not the finished whisky, because much of the smoke is lost in distillation.
Does peated whisky get smokier with age?
Generally no. Smoke is strongest in young spirit and softens over years in oak as the wood adds sweeter flavours.
